query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A CALPHAD‐based high-throughput computational screening approach can be used to design high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with enhanced phase stability, finer microstructure, and optimized properties compared to traditional synthesis methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐component high-entropy alloy system that inherently has the potential for multiple phases due to its complex composition.
generation.intervention: Application of a CALPHAD method combined with high-throughput calculations and multi-objective optimization algorithms to screen and predict optimal composition ranges.
generation.conditions: Within experimentally relevant compositional ranges (e.g., 5–50 at.% for each element) and appropriate temperature conditions as defined by the phase diagram predictions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a stable single-phase solid solution, as predicted by calculated parameters such as enthalpy of mixing, entropy of mixing, atomic size difference, and the omega parameter.
generation.mechanism: CALPHAD uses thermodynamic models to calculate key mixing parameters and phase diagrams, guiding the rapid prediction of phase stability and enabling the refinement of microstructure by discouraging formation of undesired intermetallic phases. This approach ultimately aids in achieving optimized mechanical and functional properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs designed via the CALPHAD approach will exhibit improved phase stability (i.e., predominance of a single-phase solid solution), a refined microstructure with reduced secondary phase fractions, and enhanced properties such as strength and ductility compared to alloys developed through traditional trial-and-error methods.
generation.baseline: HEAs developed via conventional methods, which may exhibit multiphase microstructures and less optimized mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the CALPHAD method depends on the quality of the underlying thermodynamic database and becomes increasingly challenging to scale for systems with more than five components or for systems with complex intermetallic formation.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvements in phase stability and mechanical properties is uncertain and may vary with the accuracy of the database and the specific alloy system under study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set designed using traditional trial-and-error approaches, and another set designed using the CALPHAD-based high-throughput screening method. Subject both sets to identical synthesis and processing conditions. Perform quantitative phase analysis (e.g., XRD) and microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/EDS) alongside mechanical property testing (yield strength, hardness, ductility).
measurements: X-ray diffraction for phase identification and quantification
Scanning electron microscopy for microstructure refinement assessment
Mechanical property tests (e.g., compressive/tensile strength, hardness measurements)
Thermophysical parameter calculations from the alloy compositions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CALPHAD-designed HEAs do not demonstrate a statistically significant enhancement in phase stability (i.e., higher single-phase fraction), microstructure refinement, or mechanical properties compared to the conventionally synthesized HEAs, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The design stage of the quinary HEA started with the calculation of the thermophysical parameters, mainly enthalpy of mixing (∆ H mix ), entropy of mixing ( Δ S mix ), atomic size difference ( δ ), and the omega parameter ( Ω ) for several compositions. The ability of a material to form a single-phase was empirically shown to depend on these three parameters. For that, the value for Δ H mix was recommended to be in the range of −15 to 5 kJ per mole, while δ should be smaller than 6.6 and Ω larger than 1.1 [26] , [27] . ∆ H mix , δ , and Ω were then calculated using Eqs. 1 – 4 respectively. Other theoretical parameters such as density ( ρ ), melting temperature ( T m ), and VEC were calculated using the rule of mixture, as shown in Eq. 5 , where i represents the element type, X represents the property, r is the atomic radius, and c represents the concentration of element i .

The atomic radii and enthalpy used in the calculations are taken from refs. [28] , [29] , respectively. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
